samples.question: This page shows one black cord that winds through several bends, plus grey cords, blue squares and orange squares as decoration. Exactly one visible gap is cut through the black cord, so the black cord falls into two separate pieces. One piece ends at the green square and the other piece ends at the red square; each anchor square covers the end of its own piece. Exactly five small orange squares are pressed against the black cord. An orange square counts only if it touches the black cord, and it then belongs to the one black piece it touches. Orange squares that touch nothing, and orange squares that touch only a grey cord, never count; blue squares never count. Straight-line distance to an anchor square is not the rule: a square belongs to the piece it is physically joined to, which you must decide by following the cord from that square past every bend until you reach either the gap or an anchor. Compare how many counting orange squares sit on the green piece with how many sit on the red piece. Does the green piece carry more counting orange squares than the red piece? Answer yes or no.
